JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN)  -- South Africa has refused the Dalai Lama a visa to attend an international peace conference in Johannesburg this week, a presidential spokesman said. The Dalai Lama fled China in 1959 after a failed uprising against Chinese rule. The Tibetan spiritual leader and Nobel Laureate did not receive a visa because it was not in South Africa's interest for him to attend, said Thabo Masebe. South Africa thinks that, if the Dalai Lama attended the conference, the focus would shift away from the 2010 World Cup -- the global soccer championship it will host next year. "We cannot allow focus to shift to China and Tibet," Masebe said, adding that South Africa has gained much from its trading relationship with China. The Dalai Lama's fellow laureate, Archbishop Desmond Tutu, said he would boycott the event.  Watch the controversy surrounding South Africa's decision » . Former president F.W. De Klerk, another laureate, backed Tutu, saying in a statement that he would also not participate in the conference if the Dalai Lama remained excluded. De Klerk said that the decision to refuse the visa made a "mockery" of the peace conference. "The decision to exclude the Dalai Lama is irreconcilable with key principles on which our society is based including the principles of accountability, openness and responsiveness and the rights to freedom of expression and free political activity," he said. "South Africa is a sovereign constitutional democracy and should not allow other countries to dictate to it regarding who it should, and should not admit to its territory - regardless of the power and influence of the country." A representative of the Dalai Lama said he was not surprised by the decision. The Tibetan government in exile thinks that China has pressured many countries to refuse a visit by the Dalai Lama, according to Chhime Chhoekyapa, an aide in Dharamsala, India. The Dalai Lama fled China in 1959 after a failed uprising against Chinese rule. The peace conference was billed as an opportunity to showcase South Africa's role as a human-rights champion ahead of its hosting of soccer's World Cup next year. It was to bring together Noble Laureates and top soccer officials. In addition to Tutu and De Klerk, laureates Nelson Mandela and Martti Ahtisaari, Sepp Blatter, president of soccer's international governing body, and actress Charlize Theron were invited to attend. The event had the blessing of the Nobel Committee.

# South Africa Denies Dalai Lama Visa, Sparking Nobel Laureate Boycott

South Africa has refused to grant the Dalai Lama a visa to attend an international peace conference in Johannesburg, a decision that has drawn sharp criticism and prompted prominent figures to withdraw from the event in protest.

The Tibetan spiritual leader had been invited to participate in the gathering, which was intended to bring together influential voices to discuss global peace and reconciliation. The refusal to admit the Dalai Lama provoked immediate outrage among fellow Nobel Peace Prize laureates. Archbishop Desmond Tutu, one of South Africa's most revered moral authorities and a longtime advocate for human rights, announced that he would boycott the conference in response. He was joined by former President F.W. de Klerk, who shared the Nobel Peace Prize with Nelson Mandela for his role in dismantling apartheid.

De Klerk was particularly forceful in his condemnation, describing the exclusion of the Dalai Lama as a "mockery" of the very peace conference the country was meant to be hosting. The controversy cast a shadow over the conference and raised broader questions about the influence of economic and diplomatic pressures on South Africa's commitment to its founding values.

# Johannesburg: The Heart of South Africa

Johannesburg, often affectionately called "Jo'burg" or "Jozi," stands as the largest city in South Africa and one of the most dynamic urban centers on the African continent. Though it is not the country's capital, it serves as the economic powerhouse of the nation and a vibrant hub of culture, commerce, and history.

## A City Born from Gold

Johannesburg's origins trace back to 1886, when gold was discovered in the Witwatersrand region. This discovery transformed a quiet stretch of land into a bustling settlement almost overnight. The promise of wealth drew people from around the world, and the city rapidly grew into a mining metropolis. Today, remnants of this golden legacy remain visible in the city's mine dumps and historical landmarks.

## Economic Significance

As the financial capital of South Africa, Johannesburg hosts the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE), the largest stock exchange on the African continent. The city contributes significantly to South Africa's gross domestic product and serves as headquarters for numerous national and multinational corporations.

## Cultural Diversity

Johannesburg is a melting pot of cultures, languages, and traditions. The city reflects South Africa's rich diversity, with residents representing various ethnic backgrounds and heritages. This blend creates a unique atmosphere found in its markets, restaurants, music venues, and neighborhoods.

## Historical Importance

The city played a pivotal role in South Africa's struggle against apartheid. Soweto, a township within greater Johannesburg, was at the center of resistance movements. Visitors today can explore important sites such as the Apartheid Museum and Constitution Hill, which offer profound insights into the nation's difficult past and its journey toward democracy.

## A Modern Metropolis

Contemporary Johannesburg balances its historical roots with modern development. Gleaming skyscrapers, shopping centers, and cultural institutions coexist alongside historic sites. The city continues to evolve, attracting entrepreneurs, artists, and visitors from across the globe.

Johannesburg remains a testament to resilience, transformation, and the enduring spirit of South Africa.

# South Africa Denies Dalai Lama Entry, Sparking Domestic and International Outcry

**Controversy erupts over visa refusal ahead of 2010 World Cup, raising questions about China's influence and South Africa's moral legacy**

## The Refusal

South Africa found itself at the center of an international controversy after its government effectively denied the Dalai Lama a visa to attend a peace conference in Johannesburg. The Tibetan spiritual leader had been invited to participate in a gathering of Nobel Peace Prize laureates, an event intended to leverage the goodwill and global attention surrounding South Africa's hosting of the 2010 FIFA World Cup to promote peace and combat racism and xenophobia.

The South African government's decision drew immediate condemnation from human rights advocates, fellow Nobel laureates, and opposition politicians who accused the ruling African National Congress (ANC) government of buckling to pressure from Beijing.

## China's Shadow

At the heart of the controversy was the widely held perception that South Africa acted to protect its growing economic relationship with China, its largest trading partner. The Dalai Lama, whom Beijing regards as a dangerous separatist seeking to split Tibet from China, has long been a diplomatic flashpoint. Countries that host him frequently face economic and diplomatic retaliation from the Chinese government.

Government officials offered various justifications for the decision, suggesting that the Dalai Lama's presence would distract attention from the World Cup and shift focus away from the football tournament that South Africa was proudly preparing to host. Critics dismissed these explanations as thin cover for a decision driven by economic self-interest and deference to Chinese pressure.

## Nobel Laureates in Revolt

The refusal provoked a powerful backlash from South Africa's own moral icons. Archbishop Desmond Tutu, the anti-apartheid hero and Nobel Peace Prize laureate, was among the most vocal critics, expressing profound disappointment and anger at the government's stance. Tutu condemned the decision as a betrayal of the values for which so many South Africans had struggled during the apartheid era.

Former President F.W. de Klerk, who shared the Nobel Peace Prize with Nelson Mandela, also expressed concern. In protest, the peace conference was ultimately postponed and thrown into disarray as laureates withdrew their participation, unwilling to attend an event from which a fellow Nobel winner had been excluded.

## A Painful Irony

Much of the criticism centered on the perceived hypocrisy of the situation. South Africa, a nation that had overcome apartheid with substantial international solidarity and moral support, was now seen as denying a peaceful religious leader the same principled stand that others had once extended to it. Commentators noted the bitter irony that a country born from a struggle for human rights and dignity would exclude a globally respected advocate for those very principles.

## Political Fallout

Opposition parties seized on the controversy to attack the government. The Democratic Alliance and other groups characterized the decision as evidence that South Africa had compromised its founding principles for commercial gain, effectively allowing a foreign power to dictate who could and could not enter the country.

The episode raised broader questions about South Africa's foreign policy direction and whether its post-apartheid commitment to human rights had become subordinate to pragmatic economic and diplomatic considerations, particularly regarding its relationships with major powers.

## Broader Context

The incident was not the first time the Dalai Lama's travel had generated diplomatic friction, and it would not be the last time South Africa faced this dilemma. In subsequent years, the country would again encounter difficulties over proposed visits by the Tibetan leader, reinforcing perceptions of a pattern of accommodation toward Beijing.

The controversy cast a shadow over what should have been a moment of unalloyed national pride, as South Africa prepared to become the first African nation to host the FIFA World Cup. Rather than celebrating its emergence on the global stage, the government found itself defending a decision that many at home and abroad viewed as a compromise of the moral authority South Africa had worked so hard to establish.

---

# South Africa's Dalai Lama Visa Denial Renews Debate Over Chinese Influence

## Nobel Laureates' Peace Gathering Overshadowed by Diplomatic Controversy

South Africa's refusal to grant a visa to the Dalai Lama sparked significant international controversy, raising pointed questions about the extent to which economic ties with China shape the foreign policy decisions of developing nations.

## The Core Controversy

The Tibetan spiritual leader was invited to attend a peace conference in South Africa alongside fellow Nobel Peace Prize laureates, including Archbishop Desmond Tutu and former President F.W. de Klerk. When South African authorities declined to process his visa, the conference organizers postponed the event, and several laureates threatened to boycott in protest.

Archbishop Tutu, one of South Africa's most revered moral voices, delivered a scathing rebuke of the government. He characterized the decision as a betrayal of the anti-apartheid struggle's legacy, suggesting the ruling African National Congress had "forgotten" the international solidarity that helped end apartheid.

## The China Factor

At the heart of the controversy lies South Africa's deepening relationship with China. Key considerations include:

- **Trade dependency**: China has become one of South Africa's largest trading partners, with billions in bilateral commerce at stake.
- **BRICS membership**: South Africa's inclusion in the emerging-economies bloc alongside Brazil, Russia, India, and China represents a significant diplomatic and economic alignment.
- **Investment flows**: Chinese infrastructure investment and loans have grown substantially across the African continent.

Beijing consistently regards the Dalai Lama as a "separatist" seeking Tibetan independence—a characterization he disputes, maintaining he seeks only genuine autonomy. China routinely applies diplomatic pressure on nations considering hosting him.

## Official Denials and Skepticism

South African government officials publicly denied that Chinese pressure influenced the visa decision, offering procedural and logistical explanations instead. Officials maintained the decision served national interests.

However, these explanations were met with widespread skepticism from opposition parties, civil society organizations, and international observers, who pointed to a pattern of similar visa complications on multiple occasions when the Dalai Lama sought entry.

## Broader Implications

The episode illuminates a tension confronting many nations in the developing world: balancing the economic benefits of Chinese partnership against commitments to human rights principles and freedom of association.

Critics argued the decision compromised South Africa's post-apartheid identity as a champion of human rights. Supporters of the government's position emphasized the practical realities of protecting vital economic relationships.

## Conclusion

The controversy ultimately transcended a single visa application, serving as a case study in how economic interdependence can shape—or appear to shape—the sovereign decisions of nations navigating an increasingly multipolar world.

---

*Note: This piece addresses events that occurred across multiple instances (notably around 2009 and 2011) when the Dalai Lama faced visa difficulties in South Africa. For a specific published article, consult primary journalistic sources for precise dates, quotations, and official statements.*

Archbishop Desmond Tutu, himself a Nobel Peace laureate and one of the country's most revered moral voices, condemned the government's decision in sharp terms. Tutu warned that South Africa was betraying the values for which so many had struggled during the anti-apartheid movement.

"We are disgraceful," Tutu said, expressing outrage that his nation would deny entry to a fellow laureate and man of peace. He suggested the government was bowing to pressure from China, a major trading partner.

Several other laureates announced they would not attend in solidarity, effectively forcing the postponement of the event. The withdrawals dealt an embarrassing blow to the summit's organizers and to South Africa's international standing.

## The China Question

Critics widely interpreted the visa denial as an effort to avoid offending Beijing, which regards the Dalai Lama as a separatist figure and routinely objects to foreign governments granting him official recognition. China has expanded its economic and diplomatic ties across Africa, and observers questioned whether commercial interests had trumped principle.

The South African government defended its position, arguing that the Dalai Lama's presence was not in the country's best interests and could distract from the summit's purpose. Officials denied that the decision was made under external pressure.

## A Blow to South Africa's Legacy

The episode struck a particularly sensitive nerve given South Africa's own history. Many of the anti-apartheid movement's leaders depended on international solidarity and moral support during their decades-long struggle. To some observers, denying entry to the Dalai Lama seemed to contradict the very principles upon which the post-apartheid nation was founded.

Human rights organizations echoed the laureates' criticism, warning that the decision damaged South Africa's credibility as a champion of freedom and justice.

## Looking Ahead

The controversy raised broader questions about how emerging economic partnerships may shape the foreign policy choices of democratic nations. For the Nobel laureates who withdrew, the message was clear: the principles of peace and human dignity cannot be set aside for political or economic convenience.
